entries_new.name: Brunei under British protection
entries_new.mechanism: A weakening ruler gave a stronger state his foreign affairs to stop his land being taken.
entries_new.story: Brunei is a sultanate on the island of Borneo that lost land to James Brooke's Sarawak and to a British chartered company in the 19th century. The Protectorate Agreement signed on 17 September 1888 stopped the sultan from ceding or leasing territory to foreign powers without British consent and gave Britain control of external affairs. The agreement did not stop Sarawak taking the Pandaruan District in 1890, and Britain added a resident adviser in 1906. Britain helped end a small armed rebellion in 1962. Protection ended on 1 January 1984 and Brunei became fully sovereign.

entries_new.name: Sikkim, protectorate to Indian state
entries_new.mechanism: A kingdom kept internal rule by treaty until the protector's army and a referendum ended it.
entries_new.story: Sikkim was a Himalayan kingdom ruled by a monarch called the Chogyal. A 1950 treaty made it an Indian protectorate: India controlled foreign affairs, defence, diplomacy and communications, and Sikkim kept control of its own administration. Anti-royalist riots took place in front of the palace in 1973. In 1975 Sikkim's prime minister, Kazi Lhendup Dorjee, asked India for statehood. In April the Indian Army took over Gangtok and disarmed the palace guards. A referendum followed in which 97.5% of voters supported abolishing the monarchy, and Sikkim became India's 22nd state.

entries_new.name: Bhutan and the Treaty of Punakha
entries_new.mechanism: A defeated kingdom handed its foreign relations to the victor and kept its own rule at home.
entries_new.story: Bhutan lost the Duar War against British India in 1864 to 1865 and gave up land under the Treaty of Sinchula. The Treaty of Punakha, signed on 8 January 1910, amended it: Britain guaranteed Bhutan's independence, raised its payment to the government and took control of its foreign relations. India recognised Bhutan's independence in a treaty of 8 August 1949 and returned the land around Deothang. A new treaty in February 2007 replaced the 1949 one and says the two governments "shall cooperate closely with each other on issues relating to their national interests". One list of protectorates puts Indian protection at 1947 to 2011.

entries_new.name: Trucial States
entries_new.mechanism: Local rulers gave Britain control of outside relations in exchange for defence, and kept their own rule.
entries_new.story: The Trucial States were sheikhdoms on the Persian Gulf coast whose leaders signed protective treaties with Britain between 1820 and 1892, starting with the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 and the Perpetual Maritime Truce of 1853. The 1892 Exclusive Agreements, following Bahrain's in 1880, put them under a status that fell short of a formal protectorate and committed Britain to defend them. The treaties were revoked on 1 December 1971. The next day six sheikhdoms formed the United Arab Emirates, and Ras Al Khaimah joined on 10 February 1972.

entries_new.name: Princely states of India
entries_new.stopped_by: Accession from 1947; abolition of the privy purses, 1971
entries_new.pop: 23% of the people of pre-independence India
entries_new.recognition: Britain, then India and Pakistan through accession
entries_new.mechanism: Local dynasties kept internal rule by accepting a stronger power's control of everything outside.
entries_new.story: A princely state was a territory in the British Indian Empire run by its own ruler, under British overlordship called paramountcy. Rulers mostly governed their own lands, but could not deal with foreign states or fight each other. When Britain left, 565 were officially recognised, covering 40% of the area of pre-independence India and 23% of its people. Nehru observed in 1946 that none could beat independent India's army. Rulers acceded to India or Pakistan and received allowances called privy purses. India abolished these in 1971, ending legal recognition of the princely order.

entries_new.name: Khanate of Kalat's independence bid
entries_new.mechanism: A protected ruler used the end of paramountcy to claim independence.
entries_new.story: Kalat was a princely state in what is now Pakistan. When Britain left, Ahmad Yar Khan, its ruler, declared independence, which was one of the options given to all princely states. It stayed independent until accession on 27 March 1948. His brother, Prince Abdul Karim, revolted against that signing in July 1948, starting an insurgency that is still unresolved.

entries_new.name: Cairo Agreement, 1969
entries_new.mechanism: A host state's army gave a refugee movement written control over camps and kept sovereignty on paper.
entries_new.story: The Cairo Agreement was a deal reached in November 1969 between Yasser Arafat and the Lebanese army commander Emile Bustani, brokered by Egypt's President Nasser. Its text was never officially published, and an unofficial version appeared in a Beirut newspaper in 1970. It took 16 UN refugee camps, home to 300,000 Palestinians, out of the jurisdiction of Lebanon's military intelligence and placed them under a PLO command, with local Palestinian committees running camp affairs "in keeping with the principle of Lebanese sovereignty". Lebanon's parliament approved a law to annul it on 21 May 1987, and President Amine Gemayel signed it that June.
entries_new.anchor: Beirut, Lebanon (the camps are across the country)

sources.t: Unofficial Text of the Cairo Agreement (Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question)

entries_new.name: Ain al-Hilweh camp
entries_new.challenge: Lebanese army offensive around Sidon, 1991; a wall from 2016
entries_new.mechanism: The host army stays outside the fence, and armed factions inside settle who governs.
entries_new.story: Ain al-Hilweh is the largest Palestinian refugee camp in Lebanon, near Sidon, set up in 1948 by the Red Cross on private land. It held over 70,000 people, rising to nearly 120,000 after refugees came from Syria. The Lebanese army does not enter, and Lebanese media call it a "zone of unlaw". Factions decide who rules inside: Fatah took control in September 1990 after a three-day fight with the Abu Nidal Organization that killed 68. Clashes with Islamist groups came in 2003, 2008 and July 2023. In 2016 Lebanon began building a concrete wall with watch towers around it.

entries_new.name: Exarcheia, Athens
entries_new.stopped_by: Evictions under the Greek government from 2019
entries_new.laws: The Academic Asylum Law barred police from campuses
entries_new.challenge: Greek police and the Ministry of Citizen's Protection
entries_new.mechanism: A university's legal immunity from police and a dense set of squats kept the state at a distance for a time.
entries_new.story: Exarcheia is a neighbourhood in central Athens beside the Polytechnic, where a 1973 student occupation ended with the army's raid. The Academic Asylum Law that followed barred police and soldiers from campuses, and the Polytechnic became a safe base for protest. After police shot a 15-year-old there in December 2008, collectives turned a parking lot into a park and started cooperatives and kitchens. More than a dozen squats, mainly here, housed refugees, migrants and anarchists. In 2019 the new prime minister pledged to "clean up" the area. Seven squats were evicted by that September, and a November order gave the rest 15 days.

entries_new.name: Mae La camp
entries_new.challenge: Armed raids in 1995 and 1997; Thai consolidation of camps
entries_new.mechanism: Refugees live inside a host-state camp supplied by aid groups, close to their own armed movement across the border.
entries_new.story: Mae La, or Beh Klaw, is the largest camp for Karen refugees from Myanmar, in Tak Province, Thailand, opened in 1984 with 1,100 people after a Karen National Union base fell. It houses about 50,000, over 90% of them Karen. Until 1995 people could travel out for food and building materials. Thai authorities then consolidated camps here after cross-border raids. Eleven aid groups in the Thailand Burma Border Consortium supply it, and it serves as a place of schooling for refugees. By June 2014, 96,206 refugees from the border camps had been resettled abroad, 75% of them in the United States.
entries_new.anchor: Tha Song Yang District, Tak, Thailand

entries_new.name: Dadaab camps
entries_new.challenge: Repeated Kenyan threats to close the camps
entries_new.mechanism: A UN agency runs a large settlement on land where the host state keeps the final say.
entries_new.story: Dadaab is a town in Garissa County, Kenya, home to a UN refugee base holding 417,767 registered refugees and asylum seekers as of 31 May 2026, most from Somalia's civil war. The camps were built in 1992. Kenya registers and fingerprints arrivals, UNHCR manages the camps, and other agencies run water, food and health care. Each camp has markets, and the Ifo II camp includes police stations and religious spaces, and many residents have built homes of mud, metal and branches. After the Garissa University attack in 2015, which killed 148, Kenya asked UNHCR to send remaining refugees to Somalia within three months. Others questioned the government's reasons for closing the camps.

entries_new.name: Kakuma camp
entries_new.mechanism: A UN-run camp becomes a town in its own right, separate from the local economy and in tension with it.
entries_new.story: Kakuma is a town in Turkana County in north-west Kenya with a UNHCR refugee camp, set up in the early 1990s for unaccompanied minors who had fled war in Sudan and Somalia, an estimated 12,000 "lost boys and girls". The town grew from about 8,000 people in 1990 to 60,000 in 2014. The camp has better clinics and school attendance than the region around it, which is the second poorest in Kenya, and that has fed tensions with local herders that have sometimes turned violent. In 2011 the World Food Programme fed 98.3% of the registered refugees.

entries_new.name: Zaatari camp
entries_new.mechanism: A temporary camp grows into a town, and the host state keeps control through leave permits.
entries_new.story: Zaatari is a refugee camp in northern Jordan, opened on 28 July 2012 for Syrians fleeing the war, and the world's largest camp for Syrian refugees. Within a few months it was the largest population centre in Mafraq Governorate. Its registered population was 79,000 in September 2014 and 77,298 on 30 September 2024. Movement out is managed through temporary leave permits. Residents have used demonstrations to protest the Syrian government. Crime grew in 2013 and a riot on 5 April 2014 killed one refugee.

entries_new.name: Yarmouk
entries_new.mechanism: A refugee district inside a capital passed between armed factions once the state lost hold of it.
entries_new.story: Yarmouk is a district of Damascus of 2.11 square km, set up in 1957 and home to the largest Palestinian refugee community in Syria, with 112,550 registered refugees in 2002. It is an unofficial camp, since UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, rejected a Syrian request to recognise it in 1960. Fighting reached it in 2012 between the Free Syrian Army and the PFLP-GC, a Palestinian faction backed by the Syrian government, and factions then took it over, with supplies cut off and hunger. The Islamic State overran most of it in April 2015. Syrian government forces took it in 2018, leaving 100 to 200 residents.

entries_new.name: Metelkova
entries_new.recognition: Recognised as national cultural heritage, with no legal status for the squat
entries_new.mechanism: People occupied state buildings and stayed, with cultural status making removal harder.
entries_new.story: Metelkova is a self-managed social centre of seven former army barracks over 12,500 square metres in central Ljubljana, Slovenia, squatted since September 1993. After independence in 1991, a network of more than 200 youth and alternative groups asked the city to use the empty barracks. In 1993 a commissioner ordered some demolished to make way for commercial use, and the groups occupied them. One building was demolished in August 2006 after several failed attempts. It has never received a proper legal status, though the area was recognised as national cultural heritage.

entries_new.name: Rote Flora
entries_new.challenge: City of Hamburg and a private owner
entries_new.cost: Sold for 370,000 DM; buy-back offer of 1.1 million euros against a 5 million asking price
entries_new.mechanism: Occupiers refused any contract and kept the building through public pressure.
entries_new.story: Rote Flora is a former theatre in Hamburg, Germany, squatted since November 1989 as a self-managed social centre. Locals feared a planned Phantom of the Opera venue would change the area, and sabotage on the building site won them a temporary lease. When it expired on 1 November 1989 they stayed. They refused a city contract in the early 1990s. Hamburg sold the building to a developer for 370,000 DM on condition that it stayed a social centre. That contract ended in 2011, and the city offered 1.1 million euros to buy it back while he asked 5 million.

entries_new.name: Calais Jungle
entries_new.mechanism: Migrants built a town with its own economy on waste land, tolerated by the state for a time.
entries_new.story: The Calais Jungle, officially Camp de la Lande, was a migrant encampment on a former landfill east of Calais, France, from January 2015 to October 2016. People stayed while trying to reach Britain or waiting on French asylum claims. It had 3,000 people by July 2015, and a census by the charity Help Refugees counted 8,143 just before the end. It held shops, restaurants, schools, places of worship and a boxing club. France first tolerated it, then evicted the southern part in February 2016 and demolished the whole camp in October 2016, with a plan to move 6,400 people to reception centres.

entries_new.name: Villa El Salvador
entries_new.mechanism: A mass land occupation built its own services and was later treated as a normal city district.
entries_new.story: Villa El Salvador is a district on the outskirts of Lima, Peru, that began in 1971 when families who had migrated from the central highlands occupied empty sand flats. The land invasion quickly made a town of 25,000, which grew to 350,000 by 2008. It was largely self-organising, and residents did much of the work to bring in electricity, water and sewage. The activist María Elena Moyano helped organise a women's federation there. It is now a district of Lima.

entries_new.name: Tonga's Treaty of Friendship, 1900
entries_new.mechanism: A king under threat from settlers and rivals gave a stronger state a veto over outside affairs.
entries_new.story: Tonga, a Pacific kingdom, became a British protected state under a Treaty of Friendship on 18 May 1900. European settlers and rival chiefs were trying to oust King George Tupou II, and Germany was gaining territory in the Pacific. Britain never ruled it directly, but its foreign affairs ran through the British consul, which gave Britain a veto over foreign policy and finances. The arrangement ended in 1970 under terms set by Queen Sālote before her death.

entries_new.name: Kuwait's 1899 agreement with Britain
entries_new.mechanism: A local ruler traded exclusive access to a stronger empire for protection against a neighbouring one.
entries_new.story: In 1899 Sheikh Mubarak Al Sabah, ruler of Kuwait, signed an agreement with the British government in India, later called the Anglo-Kuwaiti Agreement of 1899, that made Kuwait a British protectorate. Britain gained exclusive access and trade, and the Ottoman provinces to the north were denied a port on the Persian Gulf. In the First World War Britain blockaded Kuwait when a later ruler backed the Ottomans. The agreements ended in June 1961, when Kuwait became independent .

entries_new.name: Franco-Monégasque treaties
entries_new.mechanism: A very small state keeps internal rule by leaving defence and part of foreign policy to its neighbour.
entries_new.story: Monaco's sovereignty rests on treaties with France. The 1861 treaty recognised it after it gave up two towns. A July 1918 treaty provided for limited French protection and aligned Monaco's international policy with French political, military and economic interests, and the Treaty of Versailles endorsed it in 1919. A 2002 treaty says that if the Grimaldi line has no heirs Monaco stays independent and does not pass to France. France remains responsible for defence, key judges are French magistrates on loan, and Monaco consults France on some senior appointments.

entries_new.name: San Marino's conventions with Italy
entries_new.mechanism: A landlocked state keeps independence and in return accepts limits on trade set with the state around it.
entries_new.story: San Marino is a small republic entirely surrounded by Italy. It signed a Convention of Friendship with the Kingdom of Italy in 1862, after Garibaldi allowed it to remain independent, and later conventions set rules on economic life inside it. Growing tobacco and making goods under Italy's government monopoly are forbidden in San Marino. Direct imports are also barred, so goods from third countries must pass through Italy. Abraham Lincoln, made an honorary citizen, wrote back that the republic showed republican government could be "secure and enduring".

entries_new.name: Hyderabad's bid for independence, 1947 to 1948
entries_new.mechanism: The ruler tried to turn lapsed British protection into independence with a small force.
entries_new.story: Hyderabad was the wealthiest and most powerful princely state in India, ruled by the Nizam, Mir Osman Ali Khan. The Indian Independence Act of 1947 ended Britain's alliances with such states, leaving a theoretical choice of full independence. By 1948 almost all had joined India or Pakistan. The Nizam, a Muslim ruler over a largely Hindu population, chose independence and hoped to hold it with an irregular army. A demonstration by the Razakar militia forced a delay in signing a standstill agreement with India. In September 1948 India launched Operation Polo, called a "police action", and annexed the state.

entries_new.name: Moshoeshoe's request for British protection
entries_new.mechanism: A king at war asked a distant empire to take over, on conditions, to keep his land from a nearer enemy.
entries_new.story: Moshoeshoe was king of the Basotho in southern Africa, at war with the Orange Free State between 1856 and 1868. In 1865 he wrote to the Governor of Cape Colony that he was "giving myself and my country up to Her Majesty's Government under certain conditions". The territory came under British control from 1868. Rule by Cape Colony from 1871 proved unpopular and ineffective, and Basutoland passed to the Queen's direct authority in 1884 as a Crown colony, with chiefs working alongside a British commissioner. It gained independence in 1966 as present-day Lesotho, surrounded by South Africa.

entries_new.name: Treaty of Bardo, Tunisia
entries_new.mechanism: A ruler kept his title while treaties handed foreign and then domestic power to the protector.
entries_new.story: The Treaty of Bardo was signed on 12 May 1881 between France and the bey (ruler) of Tunis, Muhammed as-Sadiq. It let France control certain areas with the stated aim of restoring order and protecting the bey from opposition, and gave France responsibility for foreign policy. The La Marsa Conventions of 8 June 1883 then gave France a right to intervene in domestic affairs. The country lost almost all autonomy to the French Resident-General. One list of protectorates dates French protection to 20 March 1956.

entries_new.name: Treaty of Fes, Morocco
entries_new.mechanism: A sultan signed protection under pressure, keeping the signature on decrees and little else.
entries_new.story: The Treaty of Fes was signed under duress by Sultan Abd al-Hafid of Morocco and the French diplomat Eugène Regnault on 30 March 1912. It gave France the right to occupy parts of the country with the stated aim of protecting the sultan from opposition. The source describes real power going to France behind "the mask of indirect rule": the French Resident-General held full powers inside and outside the country, while the sultan signed decrees. A later agreement gave Spain a zone in the Rif and Cape Juby. The treaty lasted until a joint declaration of 2 March 1956.

entries_new.name: Buganda Agreement, 1900
entries_new.mechanism: A kingdom's ruler and council were kept on, in law, on condition of loyalty.
entries_new.story: The Buganda Agreement, signed in March 1900, set the terms between Britain and the Kingdom of Buganda in present-day Uganda, six years after a British protectorate was declared there. The Kabaka, the king, was recognised as ruler for as long as he stayed faithful to the British monarch, and the Lukiiko, a council of chiefs, gained legal standing. It is also called the Buganda Charter of Rights and stood for more than 50 years.

entries_new.name: Leopold of Saxe-Coburg, King of the Belgians
entries_new.mechanism: A new state chose a well-connected foreign prince to reassure the great powers.
entries_new.story: Leopold, youngest son of the Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, had married and lost the British heir, Princess Charlotte, and had turned down the throne of an independent Greece as too precarious. When Belgium broke away in 1830, its government offered him the crown because of his links with European royal houses, and because he was the British-backed candidate with no tie to France. He became the first king of the Belgians on 21 July 1831 and reigned until 1865.

entries_new.name: Karl of Hohenzollern, elected Prince of Romania
entries_new.mechanism: Politicians elected a foreign prince on the advice of a great power.
entries_new.story: After a palace coup removed Prince Alexandru Ioan Cuza, Romanian politicians looked abroad for a ruler. A first candidate, Philip, refused. Napoleon III of France then suggested Karl of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, whose father had been Minister President of Prussia. He was elected Prince of the United Principalities on 20 April 1866 and took the name Carol. Romania declared independence in May 1877, and he ruled as King from 1881 until he died in 1914. France's recommendation carried heavy weight because of its cultural influence, and Napoleon wanted a foothold on the Black Sea.

entries_new.name: Alexander of Battenberg, Prince of Bulgaria
entries_new.mechanism: An assembly elected a foreign prince, and a great power's officers removed him.
entries_new.story: Alexander of Battenberg was elected first Prince of autonomous Bulgaria by the Grand National Assembly in 1879. He dissolved the assembly the next year and suspended the constitution in 1881 as too liberal, then restored it in 1883, which set him against Russia and made him popular at home. Unification with Eastern Rumelia was achieved and recognised by the powers in 1885. A coup by pro-Russian army officers forced him out, and he abdicated in 1886.

entries_new.name: Theodore von Neuhoff, King of Corsica
entries_new.mechanism: A foreign adventurer sold rebels on foreign aid in exchange for a crown.
entries_new.story: Theodor von Neuhoff was a German adventurer who met Corsican rebels and exiles in Genoa and persuaded them he could free the island from Genoese rule if they made him king. With help from the Bey of Tunis he landed in March 1736 with military aid, and the islanders elected and crowned him. He issued edicts, founded an order of knighthood and fought the Genoese. Rebel in-fighting led to defeat, Genoa put a price on his head, and he left that November. He was arrested for debt in Amsterdam, and returned in 1738, 1739 and 1743, but Genoese and French forces held the island.

entries_new.name: Federally Administered Tribal Areas
entries_new.mechanism: The state ruled through a separate code of its own.
entries_new.story: The Federally Administered Tribal Areas were a semi-autonomous tribal region in north-western Pakistan from 1947 to 2018, made up of seven agencies and six frontier regions. The federal government ruled directly through a special code called the Frontier Crimes Regulations. On 24 May 2018 the National Assembly voted to amend the constitution to merge the region into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, and the Senate and provincial assembly followed within days, with interim rules signed by the President.

entries_new.name: Darién Gap
entries_new.challenge: Colombia and Panama claim it, with little presence
entries_new.mechanism: Terrain keeps the state away, and armed groups and migrants use the gap.
entries_new.story: The Darién Gap is a roadless stretch of rainforest on the Colombia and Panama border, the only break in the Pan-American Highway, about 106 km between Yaviza and Turbo. Embera-Wounaan and Guna peoples live there, about 8,000 in 1995. Sources say law enforcement and medical support are nonexistent, with drug and human trafficking widespread. FARC, the Colombian guerrilla group, operated on both sides of the border. Crossings rose from 24,000 in 2019 to more than 520,000 in 2023. Environmental and Indigenous groups have opposed finishing the road.

entries_new.name: Polahi of Gorontalo
entries_new.mechanism: Ancestors fled into forest to avoid colonial rule, and their descendants stayed.
entries_new.story: The Polahi are an isolated people in the interior forests of Gorontalo on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi. According to their own stories they were fugitives who withdrew into the forest around the 17th century, out of fear of the Dutch and a refusal to be colonised. They remain isolated in the forests of Boliyohuto, Paguyaman and Suwawa.

entries_new.name: Khun Sa's Mong Tai Army
entries_new.challenge: Myanmar's army and the United Wa State Army
entries_new.mechanism: An armed force held territory near the Thai border and financed itself partly through narcotics.
entries_new.story: The Mong Tai Army was a Shan insurgent group in Myanmar, founded in 1985 by Khun Sa and based at Ho Mong near the Thai border. It had up to 20,000 troops at its peak, was among the largest forces opposing the government, and was involved in the drug trade. It fought both the government and the United Wa State Army. After an internal split in July 1995, when 8,000 fighters broke away, most laid down arms and surrendered to the government, while about 3,000 formed a new faction later called the Shan State Army-South.

entries_new.name: Makhnovshchina
entries_new.mechanism: In a war with several collapsing governments, an armed peasant movement ran local councils on the land it held.
entries_new.story: The Makhnovshchina was a mass movement for anarchist communism in southern and eastern Ukraine during the Ukrainian War of Independence of 1917 to 1921, named after Nestor Makhno, commander of the Revolutionary Insurgent Army. Its aim was a system of free soviets, or local councils, as a route to a stateless and classless society. It set up farm communes in Huliaipole, Makhno's home town. It fought the Austro-German occupiers, and at different times sided with and against the Bolsheviks. The Red Army attacked it again after the Whites were beaten and defeated it by August 1921. Leaders were exiled or killed.

entries_new.name: Montana Freemen
entries_new.stopped_by: FBI standoff, surrender on 14 June 1996, prison sentences
entries_new.mechanism: A group refused foreclosure, named its farm a township and held its own trials.
entries_new.story: The Montana Freemen were an anti-government group based outside the town of Jordan, Montana, who called their land "Justus Township" and declared themselves sovereign citizens under no outside government. They were direct descendants of the Posse Comitatus movement. They held mock trials of public officials and issued a writ of execution against a federal judge, and foreclosure proceedings began on their farm in late 1994. An FBI sting on their financial schemes led to arrests in March 1996 and an armed standoff. They surrendered after 81 days on 14 June 1996. LeRoy Schweitzer received 22 years and died in federal prison.

entries_new.name: Washitaw Nation
entries_new.recognition: None; its UN registration claim is the group's own
entries_new.mechanism: A group adopts the name of an old tribe and declares itself sovereign.
entries_new.story: The Washitaw Nation is an African-American group linked with the Moorish Science Temple that claims to be a sovereign state of Native Americans inside the United States, taking its name from the Ouachita tribe. It was headed by Verdiacee Goston, who served as mayor of Richwood, Louisiana, and styled herself Empress. She said the UN "registers the Washitaw as indigenous people No. 215". In 1999 the Southern Poverty Law Center estimated about 200 hardcore members. Its legal theory is that people can declare sovereignty and separate themselves from state and federal law. It is classed as part of the sovereign citizen movement.

zones_new.name: Places a state has never ruled in practice
zones_new.who_owns: A national government on paper, in every case listed here. India claims North Sentinel, and Brazil, Peru, Ecuador and others hold Indigenous territories under their own law. The people living there may never have dealt with those governments.

rules.cite: Andaman and Nicobar Islands Protection of Aboriginal Tribes Regulation, 1956
rules.says: Declared North Sentinel Island a tribal reserve and prohibited travel within 5 km of it.
Separates Indigenous peoples in isolation from those in initial contact, gives each different protection, and sets up an official register of these peoples and their reserves.
Requires untouchability, self-determination, equality and no contact for the Tagaeri and Taromenane in Yasuní.

rules.cite: UN Human Rights Council guidelines, 2009, and Inter-American Commission on Human Rights recommendations, 2013
rules.says: Include a right to choose self-isolation.

zones_new.hook: Some peoples and regions have never been ruled in daily practice by the state that claims them, and that gap comes from their own refusal, terrain or distance rather than from any grant of independence.
zones_new.can_you_build: No outsider can settle these places: the peoples concerned already live there, entering their land is banned in several countries, and contact has killed many of them through disease. The rest, such as the Darién Gap and the old tribal areas of Pakistan, stayed under state title, and that title was used when the state wanted it.
facts: Survival International's 2025 report: at least 196 uncontacted peoples in ten countries, 124 of them in Brazil.
Survival predicts almost half could be wiped out within 10 years if nothing changes.
Panará: of more than 350 people, more than 250 died within a year of first contact after a road came through in 1973.
Vale do Javari, Brazil: 85,444 square km declared sealed off.
Southeast Asian Massif, which overlaps Zomia: about 100 million Indigenous people.
zones_new.essay:
Uncontacted peoples are Indigenous groups who live without sustained relations with the outside world. Most have some awareness of it, and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights calls them peoples "in voluntary isolation". In 2025 Survival International published the first worldwide report on them. It found robust evidence of 196 uncontacted peoples in ten countries, with 124 groups in Brazil. They never declared a state, and none is recognised as one. Each lives on land that a national government claims.

North Sentinel Island shows the arrangement most clearly. India counts it as part of its Andaman and Nicobar Islands. A 1956 regulation made it a tribal reserve, banned travel within 5 km, and India keeps an armed patrol around it. Indian visits stopped in 1997. An American missionary who went illegally in 2018 was killed, and another American who landed in 2025 was arrested. No Indian official governs the island in daily life, and Indian law supplies the fence around it.

Brazil tried the opposite first. In the 1960s and 1970s it attempted to assimilate Amazon peoples so their land could be farmed. In 1987 it created a Department of Isolated Indians within its Indigenous affairs agency and sealed off the 85,444 square km Vale do Javari. The Panará show why: a government road reached them in 1973, and of more than 350 people, more than 250 died within a year. The Nukak of Colombia lost more than half their number after contact, and the government then moved them by force. Survival warns that almost half of the 196 could be wiped out within 10 years, and names logging, mining, and oil and gas as the main threats.

A second group of cases concerns hill country. The historian Willem van Schendel coined the name Zomia in 2002 for highlands that lowland governments had not controlled. James C. Scott argued in 2009 that its peoples were communities that had fled slavery, conscription and taxes over two millennia, and that this is coming to an end. Pakistan's tribal areas sat under a separate code, the Frontier Crimes Regulations, from 1947 until a constitutional amendment merged them into a province in 2018. Khun Sa's army held part of Myanmar until it surrendered in the mid 1990s. The Darién Gap has no road and, by one account, no law enforcement, while still lying inside Panama and Colombia.

The pattern across these cases is that distance from the state lasts until a road, a licence or a constitutional vote arrives. None of them gives a route for newcomers, and contact itself does harm. Entries for uncontacted peoples are pinned to regions only.

sources.t: What to know about the Survival International report (CBS News)
Indigenous people in isolation and initial contact in Peru (Minority Rights Group)

odds.why: An outside group cannot enter these lands lawfully, and entering would endanger the people there. Existing peoples hold their land in practice but under state title, and Survival International forecasts that almost half may not last 10 years.

own.own_why: A private group gets nothing here: the land is taken by people who already live on it, and any new settlers would meet both state law and harm to those peoples. For an existing people, the record does give decades of daily self-rule on North Sentinel and in the Vale do Javari. It falls short because it rests on state tolerance and because Survival's own forecast is that almost half could be wiped out in 10 years.

zones_new.name: When the state falls and nobody replaces it
zones_new.who_owns: The collapsed state keeps its legal title, even when it controls little. Those who hold the ground are clans, courts, militias or rebel governments, and other countries usually go on treating the old borders as valid.

rules.says: Defines a state by a permanent population, a defined territory, government and capacity to deal with other states, and says the political existence of a state is independent of recognition by other states.
Lebanese parliamentarians agreed a national reconciliation accord at Ta'if in Saudi Arabia. It laid the foundation for ending the war, and most militias were disbanded after 1990.
Called for deploying foreign troops in Somalia and lifting the arms embargo, which the Islamic Courts called an act of war.
Rival Libyan camps agreed to unite as the internationally recognised Government of National Accord.

zones_new.hook: When a government falls, whoever holds the ground may run courts, money and services for years, but outside powers keep the old state's borders and usually return to them.
zones_new.can_you_build: Armed groups have done it, and the record is of war crimes trials, foreign invasions and absorption back into the state. No private group has held a place this way without drawing on an existing people or army, and armed takeover is a crime in all the places involved.
facts: Somalia: no central government from 1991, with transitional governments from 2000 and 2004.
Greater Liberia held 90% of the country at its peak, with its own currency and banks.
Lebanon's cantons: 1976 to about 1990, ended after the 1989 Taif Agreement.
Idlib's Salvation Government had over 4 million people in 2023, and its ministers took the same posts in Syria's caretaker government in December 2024.
Viv Ansanm controls about 80% of metropolitan Port-au-Prince.
zones_new.essay:
A collapsed state is one whose government has stopped working over most of its land, with no replacement agreed. Under the Montevideo Convention of 1933, a state needs a population, a territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other states. Article 3 says a state's political existence does not depend on other states recognising it. In practice, states that collapse keep their title, because other governments carry on treating the old borders as valid, and new groups on the ground go unrecognised.

Somalia is the longest case. Clan-based groups overthrew Siad Barre in 1991. Customary law broke down in 1990 to 1992 and factions fought, and UN missions came in 1992 and left in 1995. After that, customary and religious law came back in most regions, and SIPRI, a peace research institute, dropped Somalia from its list of major conflicts for 1997 and 1998. The local system, Xeer, uses elders as mediators and compensation paid by kin groups. In Mogadishu Sharia courts formed to keep order and united by 2000. They defeated a CIA-backed warlord alliance in 2006 and governed most of the south and centre, until Ethiopia invaded that December.

Lebanon during its civil war split into militia zones called cantons. The Lebanese Forces held East Beirut and the Progressive Socialist Party held the Chouf, each with its own administration. A TIME reporter in 1976 found cleaner streets and cheaper petrol in the Christian canton than in West Beirut. The 1989 Taif Agreement ended this, and most militias disbanded. Libya after 2014 had two parliaments with allied armies and foreign backers, until a 2020 ceasefire and a 2021 interim government.

Some rebel zones become the state itself. Charles Taylor's Greater Liberia had a capital at Gbarnga, a justice system, its own currency and exports of diamonds and timber, and Taylor then won the war and the presidency. The Syrian Salvation Government, set up by the armed group HTS in Idlib in 2017, handed its ministers to the national caretaker government after Damascus fell in 2024. The Makhnovist movement in Ukraine ran local councils in the name of anarchism, and the Red Army had defeated it by August 1921.

In all of these the people doing the governing were an existing community or an armed movement, and the outcome turned on war and on foreign states. Haiti's gang coalition Viv Ansanm now controls about 80% of metropolitan Port-au-Prince, with UN-authorised forces sent against it. These records describe what happened to those places and carry heavy costs for their residents, and do not give anyone a safe or lawful way to found a place.

odds.why: Land can be held in a collapse only by those who already have fighters and a following, and the record ends mostly in defeat, absorption or takeover of the whole state. Recognition is rarely given.

own.own_why: A private group would get a short period of control in a war, at the price of serious crime. That falls short because holding for 10 years has gone to clans and armed movements with local roots, and even those mostly ended in foreign invasion or absorption. For an existing people the figure is higher: Somaliland and Puntland have run their own governments for decades with no general recognition.

zones_new.name: Refugee camps and squats that rule themselves
zones_new.who_owns: The host country, and sometimes private landowners. In Ain al-Hilweh the land belongs to villagers and townspeople of Miye ou Miye, Darb es Sim and Sidon. UN agencies run many camps, and a city or developer usually holds title to squatted buildings.

rules.says: Set up local Palestinian committees in camps in Lebanon "in keeping with the principle of Lebanese sovereignty", and armed struggle posts inside them.

rules.cite: Lebanese law annulling the Cairo Agreement, 1987
rules.says: Parliament approved it on 21 May 1987 and President Amine Gemayel signed it that June.
Every refugee has duties to the host country, in particular to conform to its laws and regulations and to measures for public order.
Designated university campuses as off-limits to police and military personnel.

zones_new.hook: Refugee camps and squats can govern daily life for decades when the host state stays outside, and every one of them sits inside a host state's legal title and can be walled, cleared or evicted.
zones_new.can_you_build: People can and do occupy buildings or build camps, usually breaking property law, and some have stayed more than 30 years. None has gained courts or laws that the surrounding state must accept, and refugees remain bound by the host's law under the 1951 Convention.
facts: Ain al-Hilweh: over 70,000 people, up to nearly 120,000, with no Lebanese army inside.
Dadaab: 417,767 registered refugees and asylum seekers as of 31 May 2026.
Rote Flora, Hamburg: squatted since November 1989.
Metelkova, Ljubljana: squatted since September 1993.
Villa El Salvador, Lima: 25,000 in a land occupation of 1971 grew to 350,000 by 2008.
zones_new.essay:
A camp or squat begins as a place where people live without permission, or with only temporary permission. Few intend to create a country, yet they can come to govern daily life, and the question is how far that goes.

The fullest legal grant came in Lebanon. The Cairo Agreement of November 1969, between Yasser Arafat and the Lebanese army commander, moved 16 UN refugee camps with 300,000 people from the army's intelligence service to a PLO command. Its unofficial text sets up local committees in the camps "in keeping with the principle of Lebanese sovereignty". The text was never officially published. Lebanon annulled the agreement by a law signed in 1987. Yet in Ain al-Hilweh near Sidon the Lebanese army still does not enter, and Fatah and Islamist groups have fought over control, most recently in July 2023. In 2016 Lebanon began building a wall around the camp. Armed factions run things inside, the state controls the perimeter, and the camp's land belongs to private owners.

Other camps are more formally run. Dadaab in Kenya had 417,767 registered refugees and asylum seekers in May 2026. Kenya registers arrivals, UNHCR manages the camps, and agencies run water, food and health. Kenya has repeatedly threatened to close them, and in 2015 it asked UNHCR to send people back to Somalia within three months. Mae La in Thailand, about 50,000 people, is supplied by aid groups, and Thai authorities moved other camps into it after raids in 1995. Zaatari in Jordan had 77,298 registered residents in 2024, and leave is managed through temporary permits. Refugees remain subject to host-country law under Article 2 of the 1951 Refugee Convention.

City squats face property owners and police. Rote Flora in Hamburg has been held since 1989, turning down a city contract and outlasting a sale to a developer. Metelkova in Ljubljana has been held since 1993, and has cultural heritage status and no proper legal status. Exarcheia in Athens drew on a law barring police from campuses, and more than a dozen squats operated there until a new government started evictions in 2019. The Calais Jungle reached 8,143 people in a charity's count, with shops and schools, and France demolished it in October 2016.

Time can bring acceptance. Villa El Salvador began as a land occupation outside Lima in 1971 and grew to 350,000, building its own services, and it is now a city district. Yarmouk in Damascus shows the opposite, with an unofficial camp of 112,550 registered refugees reduced to 100 to 200 people by 2018 during the Syrian war. In each case the place survives only as long as the state around it chooses or is unable to act.

sources.t: Unofficial Text of the Cairo Agreement
UNHCR: The Refugee Convention, 1951, with commentary

odds.why: Occupying a building or camp is easy and some last decades, but it stays under the host's law and title, and eviction is always possible. No state recognises a camp or squat as outside its law.

own.own_why: You get a building or camp where the police rarely come, sometimes for 30 years, as at Rote Flora and Metelkova. It falls short because criminal law, title and tax still belong to the host, and the state can act when it chooses, as in Calais and Athens. Ain al-Hilweh goes furthest for an existing people, and it has a wall around it and factions fighting inside.

zones_new.name: Inheriting, marrying or being chosen as ruler
zones_new.who_owns: The state in question. The ruler holds an office inside it, by inheritance, election or foreign appointment, and usually does not own the land itself.

rules.says: Set up the Kingdom of Greece, with Otto of Bavaria as king, under the three powers that guaranteed its independence.
Recognised Albania's independence. Prince Wilhelm cited Albanian neutrality under it when refusing to send soldiers in 1914.
Passed by Henry of Valois, the first elected king of the final system, they solidified a process of free election that stayed stable for two centuries.
Monaco stays an independent nation if there are no Grimaldi heirs, and does not revert to France.

zones_new.hook: Foreign princes have been handed whole countries by assemblies and great powers, and the throne then lasted only if local politics and the sponsoring powers held up.
zones_new.can_you_build: There is almost no route today: Malaysia's elective monarchy picks from nine fixed families, and the last offers to foreign princes in these records date from 1918. Claiming a title with no one behind you is what the Otto Witte story amounts to.
facts: Wilhelm of Wied held Albania from 7 March to 3 September 1914.
Three German-related thrones were offered in 1918: Lithuania, Finland and the Baltic Duchy. None was taken up in practice.
Bernadotte, a French marshal, was elected Swedish crown prince in 1810, and the dynasty continues.
Maximilian of Mexico: installed 1864, executed 1867.
Monaco: seized 1297, bought from Aragon 1419.
zones_new.essay:
For most of European history a country's ruler could come from outside it. A new state might want a neutral prince, or great powers might agree on one, and a family could also gain a place by marriage, purchase or adoption.

Being chosen by foreign powers is the clearest route. After Greece gained independence, the Convention of London made Otto of Bavaria king in 1832, aged 17, with a Bavarian regency. Britain, France and Russia guaranteed the state, and Greek parties formed around them. He was deposed in 1862. Six Great Powers selected Prince Wilhelm of Wied for Albania in 1913. He lasted six months in 1914, leaving when his foreign pay stopped. Maximilian of Austria accepted Mexico from conservative monarchists with a French army behind him. When France withdrew from 1866, republicans captured and executed him in 1867.

Elections brought outsiders too. Sweden's Riksdag elected the French marshal Jean Bernadotte as crown prince in 1810, and he was adopted by the childless king. His dynasty continues. Norway elected Prince Carl of Denmark after a referendum in 1905. Belgium chose Leopold of Saxe-Coburg in 1831 for his royal links and British backing. Romania took Karl of Hohenzollern on French advice in 1866. Bulgaria's assembly elected Alexander of Battenberg in 1879, and pro-Russian officers forced him out in 1886. Poland ran elections for a monarch until 1791, and foreign candidates made them a multinational contest. In Malaysia today nine hereditary state rulers elect one of their own as king.

The year 1918 produced a cluster of failures, because German-backed states needed monarchs. The Council of Lithuania elected Wilhelm of Urach as Mindaugas II, and Finland elected Frederick Charles of Hesse. Baltic Germans in Riga offered the Duke of Mecklenburg a throne. German authorities declared the Lithuanian election invalid, Frederick Charles renounced Finland's throne in December 1918, and Germany's defeat ended the Baltic duchy.

Family ownership is rarer. The Grimaldis captured Monaco in 1297 by posing as monks and bought it from the Crown of Aragon in 1419. Their position survives through treaties with France, including one in 2002 settling what happens if heirs run out. 

Adventurers tried a shorter route. Theodor von Neuhoff, a German baron, persuaded Corsican rebels in 1736 to crown him in return for foreign help, and he left the island within months. Otto Witte, a circus acrobat, told a story of ruling Albania for five days in 1913, which was found to be mostly impossible, though Berlin police let his identity card say "former King of Albania". A ruler needs a body that can choose him and a force that will keep him, and a title alone has neither.

odds.why: These routes need a throne on offer, and hardly any are left. Those who got one held it only with a body that chose them and a power that kept them there.

own.own_why: Being chosen would give you an existing state with courts and laws, which is much more than most routes give. It falls short because no assembly or power now offers thrones to outsiders, and the historic record ends in exile or execution as often as in a dynasty. Monaco's Grimaldis kept their place by giving up land and foreign-policy freedom to France.

zones_new.name: Asking a stronger state to be protector
zones_new.who_owns: The protected ruler on paper. The treaty leaves land and internal rule with the local state and passes foreign relations, defence or both to the protector.

rules.says: The sultan could not cede or lease territory to foreign powers without British consent, and Britain took over Brunei's foreign affairs.
Britain guaranteed Bhutan's independence, raised its stipend and took control of its foreign relations.
Ended Britain's alliances with the princely states, leaving them a theoretical choice of full independence.
The two governments "shall cooperate closely with each other on issues relating to their national interests", and neither may let its territory be used against the other's security.
Established the French protectorate in Morocco, with the Resident-General holding powers inside and outside the country and the sultan signing decrees.

zones_new.hook: Rulers have kept their thrones by giving a stronger state their foreign relations, and the same treaties have let protectors take over everything else.
zones_new.can_you_build: Every protected state began as an existing ruler with an existing people, so a new private group has nothing a protector would want and no standing to sign. Today's nearest cases, Bhutan, Monaco and San Marino, are old states with long treaties and little room to change them.
facts: 565 princely states were officially recognised when Britain left India, covering 40% of the area and 23% of the people.
Sikkim: protectorate from 1950, absorbed into India in 1975 after a referendum with 97.5% support for ending the monarchy.
Brunei: protected 1888 to 1984.
Tonga: 1900 to 1970.
Kuwait: 1899 to 1961.
zones_new.essay:
A protectorate is a state that keeps self-government over most internal affairs and accepts a treaty binding it to a stronger state on foreign policy. Writers separate this from a "protected state", which keeps its international standing and some independent foreign policy. Such relationships are often described with polite terms, such as "an independent state with special treaty relations".

The people who asked for protection usually had a specific enemy. Brunei's sultan signed in 1888 after losing land to Sarawak. Britain then took charge of foreign affairs, and when Sarawak took another district in 1890, did not act. Protection still ended on 1 January 1984 with Brunei sovereign. Tonga's king signed in 1900 with settlers and rival chiefs against him and Germany expanding in the Pacific, and left in 1970. Sheikh Mubarak of Kuwait signed in 1899, giving Britain exclusive access and keeping out the Ottomans. The Trucial sheikhs signed from 1820 to 1892, and six of them formed the UAE in 1971, the day after the treaties ended. Moshoeshoe of the Basotho wrote in 1865 that he was giving himself and his country up on conditions, to escape war with the Orange Free State. Basutoland became independent as Lesotho in 1966.

Other treaties gave up far more. Tunisia's ruler signed the Treaty of Bardo in 1881, and an 1883 convention gave France a right to intervene at home. Morocco's sultan signed the Treaty of Fes under duress in 1912. One account calls what followed "the mask of indirect rule". Sikkim shows how a protector can absorb its partner. India took over its foreign affairs and defence in 1950, its army took over Gangtok in April 1975, and a referendum ended the monarchy.

India itself was the largest case. When Britain left, 565 princely states were recognised, and the 1947 Act ended their treaties, leaving a theoretical option of independence. Nehru had said in 1946 that none could resist independent India's army. The Nizam of Hyderabad tried, and India annexed the state in September 1948. Kalat declared independence and acceded to Pakistan in March 1948. India abolished the rulers' allowances in 1971, which ended their legal recognition.

Some arrangements have lasted. Bhutan's treaty of 1910 was followed by treaties with India in 1949 and 2007. Monaco's treaties with France cover defence and foreign policy, and San Marino's conventions with Italy limit its trade. Andorra's co-princes, the bishop of Urgell and the president of France, date from a treaty of 1278, and that case is listed separately. Each protected party was already a recognised ruler or state when it signed.

odds.why: The record shows real holding and recognition for those who had a state to protect. A newcomer has no standing to sign, and no great power has a reason to offer protection today.

own.own_why: A protector could give you security and a door to the outside world while you run your own courts. It falls short because the protector can override you, as India did in Sikkim and Hyderabad, and because every past case started with an existing ruler. Existing peoples with an old ruler have a better record, though few are left without a state.

zones_new.name: Legal continuity and sovereign citizen claims
zones_new.who_owns: The existing state, with no change. Followers claim an old state, treaty or status overrides the current government, and they hold no territory beyond private homes and farms they own or occupy.

rules.cite: Meads v Meads, 2012 ABQB 571, Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta
rules.says: A claim to a status that lets someone ignore a court is wrong in law and may be struck out. The judge called such strategies "little more than scams that abuse legal process".
Whatever someone calls themselves, be it "sovereign citizen" or "flesh-and-blood human being", they remain subject to the court.
The plaintiff "is not a sovereign citizen. He is a U.S. citizen ... and has no immunity from U.S. law".

rules.cite: German federal ban on Königreich Deutschland, 13 May 2025
rules.says: The Interior Ministry banned the group as a "counter-state", with online platforms blocked and assets confiscated.

zones_new.hook: These claims say an old state or a technical status still exempts someone from the law, and courts in every country where they have been tried have rejected them.
zones_new.can_you_build: Nothing is created by filing the paper: no court anywhere has accepted these claims, and followers have been jailed for fraud, tax evasion and threats. The groups that bought land and ran their own money, as in Germany and Montana, drew bans, an FBI siege and long sentences.
facts: German domestic intelligence estimated about 21,000 Reichsbürger as of July 2021.
Königreich Deutschland: about 1,000 members by official count, 6,000 by its own claim.
Montana Freemen: surrendered after 81 days on 14 June 1996.
Bey v. Indiana: $11.5 billion demanded, suit called frivolous.
Meads v Meads: a 188-page judgment arising from a divorce.
zones_new.essay:
This family of claims says that the state people live under is not legally what it appears to be, or does not apply to them. Sovereign citizens in the United States say statutes bind only those who consent. Freemen on the land say the same in Canada and elsewhere in the Commonwealth. Germany's Reichsbürger, or Reich Citizens, say the German Reich never legally ended. Moorish sovereign citizens say a 1786 treaty with Morocco makes them a separate nation. These arguments have no basis in law and have never succeeded in court.

The sovereign citizen movement began in the early 1970s, with roots in far-right groups such as the Posse Comitatus. Its ideas have spread to Canada, Australia, Britain and New Zealand, and into groups with very different origins. The FBI classifies "sovereign citizen extremists" as domestic terrorists, while most followers are not violent. Many have been convicted of tax evasion, forgery, threats and bank fraud.

Courts have written their replies with care. In United States v. Benabe in 2011 a US appeals court said a claimed status as a sovereign citizen or a flesh-and-blood human being does not remove a person from the court's power. In Meads v Meads in 2012, Associate Chief Justice John Rooke of Alberta used a divorce case to gather all such arguments under the name Organized Pseudolegal Commercial Argument and to refute them over 188 pages. Courts in Canada and other Commonwealth countries now use it. In Bey v. Indiana in 2017 the Seventh Circuit explained the Moorish theory so other courts would not need to look into it again, and rejected an $11.5 billion demand. It noted that the Moorish Science Temple says it is no sovereign citizen or tax protest movement.

Trouble comes when a group acts on the claim. The Montana Freemen named their farm Justus Township, held mock trials of officials and issued a writ against a federal judge. They surrendered after an 81-day FBI standoff in 1996, and one received 22 years. Bruce Doucette, a self-styled judge, set up "common law courts" and was sentenced in 2018. In December 2022 Germany arrested 25 people accused of planning a coup that would have made Heinrich XIII Prinz Reuss head of state.

The largest attempt at a working parallel state was Königreich Deutschland, proclaimed by Peter Fitzek in Wittenberg in 2012, which had its own constitution and identity papers. Prosecutors allege it swapped euros for its own currency with no right of return and ran banking and insurance without licences, and that it bought property in three German states. Germany banned it on 13 May 2025, and four alleged leaders have been charged. Buying land gives a group ordinary property rights under the law it rejects.

sources.t: Alberta Court Skewers Gibberish Legal Arguments (Bennett Jones)
Seventh Circuit Denounces 'Sovereign Citizen' Claims (Prison Legal News)
Germany bans the far-right 'Kingdom of Germany' group (AP via AOL)

odds.why: Courts have rejected the arguments every time. Any group acting on them has faced prosecution or a ban, and no state has recognised one.

own.own_why: You get a document and sometimes a purchased farm, with nothing that binds a court. It falls short because the land stays under the law the group rejects, and those who acted on the claim, in Montana and in Germany, ended in prison or under a ban.
